label: the genitive suffix itself: -nre / -ude on any noun
note: Chapter 78. The note was exact: enre and ninre were taught WHOLE and the suffix inside them was never named, so the learner owned two possessors and could not make a third. Naming it turns a closed pair into an open rule -- any taught noun can now own something. BOTH ALLOMORPHS are taught, one per lesson, because the choice is not the speaker's: -nre after a consonant (adhyaapakan-re), -yude after a vowel (ammayude). Verified before writing: NO third genitive existed anywhere in the corpus, so teaching the suffix here created no forward reference -- the only bare -nre token was the script decomposition inside ML-C02-enre, which showed the conjunct as a SHAPE. The chapter says so: something introduced as a shape often turns out later to be a part.
